subject: Physics
description: Reflection of light — laws, plane and curved mirrors, image formation, applications (periscope, kaleidoscope), mirror formula.

questions.stem: The FIRST LAW of REFLECTION states that the angle of incidence:

options.option_text: Is twice the angle of reflection
Is half the angle of reflection

questions.explanation: LAWS OF REFLECTION (memorize): (1) ANGLE OF INCIDENCE (i) = ANGLE OF REFLECTION (r), measured from the NORMAL (perpendicular to surface). (2) Incident ray, reflected ray, and normal LIE IN THE SAME PLANE. KEY: angles measured from NORMAL (NOT from the surface). NORMAL = imaginary line PERPENDICULAR to surface at point of incidence. BOTH LAWS apply equally to PLANE MIRRORS, CURVED MIRRORS, and even DIFFUSE reflection from rough surfaces (locally for each tiny smooth part). REGULAR vs DIFFUSE REFLECTION: (1) REGULAR (specular) — smooth surface (mirror, polished metal, still water) → parallel rays remain parallel; CLEAR IMAGE. (2) DIFFUSE — rough surface (paper, cloth, walls) → parallel rays scatter in many directions; NO IMAGE. WHY WE SEE OBJECTS: light from sources reflects DIFFUSELY off everyday objects → reaches our eyes → brain forms image. ANIMAL EYE-SHINE: many nocturnal animals (cats, dogs, deer) have TAPETUM LUCIDUM behind retina — reflects light back through retina → glow in dark. PYQ FREQUENCY: laws of reflection in NEET, NCERT 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: Image formed by a PLANE MIRROR is:
questions.explanation: PLANE MIRROR image properties: (1) VIRTUAL (cannot be projected on screen; rays only appear to come from behind mirror). (2) ERECT (right-side up). (3) SAME SIZE as object. (4) AT EQUAL DISTANCE behind mirror as object is in front. (5) LATERALLY INVERTED — left-right flipped. (NOT top-bottom flipped — this is a common misconception.) LATERAL INVERSION explains: (a) text appears reversed in mirror. (b) AMBULANCE has 'AMBULANCE' written in REVERSE on its front so drivers see it correctly in their REARVIEW MIRROR. (c) Right hand appears as left hand in mirror. SAMPLE MIRROR experiments: 'YOGA' written in mirror image looks like 'AGOY' (mirror flip). NUMBER 1881 looks like '1881' in mirror (palindrome by mirror). USES of PLANE MIRRORS: bathroom mirror, full-length dressing mirror, periscopes (with two), kaleidoscopes (with three at angles). MULTIPLE-MIRROR IMAGES: number of images = (360°/θ) − 1, where θ = angle between two mirrors. e.g., θ=90° → 3 images; θ=60° → 5; θ=30° → 11. KALEIDOSCOPE typically uses 60° angle → 6 images forming a star pattern. PYQ FREQUENCY: plane mirror properties in NEET, NCERT, JEE-Main 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: A CONCAVE MIRROR is also called a CONVERGING MIRROR because:

options.option_text: It converges parallel rays to focus

questions.explanation: CONCAVE MIRROR — reflective surface CURVED INWARD (like the inside of a sphere). Parallel rays of light entering a CONCAVE mirror converge to a single point — the FOCAL POINT (F). Hence 'CONVERGING' mirror. FOCAL LENGTH (f) = distance from mirror to focal point; f = R/2 (where R = radius of curvature). KEY POINTS on CONCAVE mirror: (1) POLE (P) — center of mirror surface. (2) CENTER OF CURVATURE (C) — center of the sphere from which the mirror is cut. (3) FOCUS (F) — halfway between P and C. (4) PRINCIPAL AXIS — line through P and C. IMAGE FORMATION depends on object distance: (a) Object beyond C: real, inverted, smaller. (b) At C: real, inverted, same size. (c) Between F and C: real, inverted, larger. (d) At F: image at infinity (parallel rays). (e) Between F and P: virtual, erect, larger (used for shaving/makeup mirrors!). USES OF CONCAVE MIRRORS: (1) SHAVING/MAKEUP mirrors (object closer than F gives magnified erect image). (2) DENTIST MIRRORS. (3) HEADLIGHTS, FLASHLIGHTS, search lights — light source at focus → parallel beam emerges. (4) SOLAR cookers, solar furnaces. (5) ASTRONOMICAL TELESCOPES (Newtonian, Cassegrain). (6) Reflectors in operating-theater lights. PYQ FREQUENCY: concave mirror in NEET, NCERT 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: An object 4 cm tall is placed 30 cm in front of a CONCAVE MIRROR of focal length 15 cm. Image position is:
questions.explanation: Apply MIRROR FORMULA: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f (Cartesian convention; u = object distance, v = image distance, f = focal length, with appropriate signs). For CONCAVE MIRROR: f is NEGATIVE (in many conventions); u is NEGATIVE (object in front). Plug u = −30, f = −15: 1/v + 1/(−30) = 1/(−15) → 1/v = 1/(−15) + 1/30 = −2/30 + 1/30 = −1/30 → v = −30 cm. v negative → image is in FRONT of mirror (REAL image). DISTANCE: 30 cm. INTERPRETATION: object at 2F → image also at 2F (same distance), inverted, real, same size. MIRROR FORMULA: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f. MAGNIFICATION: m = −v/u = h_image/h_object. Plug m = −(−30)/(−30) = 30/(−30) = −1 → image inverted, same size as object (4 cm). KEY CASES for concave mirror: object at 2F → image at 2F, real, inverted, same size. Object beyond 2F → image between F and 2F, real, inverted, smaller. Object between F and 2F → image beyond 2F, real, inverted, larger. Object at F → image at infinity. Object inside F → image behind mirror, virtual, erect, larger (e.g., shaving mirror). NUMERICAL PRACTICE in NEET, JEE-Main 2-3× per paper. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests sign convention + formula application.

questions.stem: REAR-VIEW MIRRORS in cars and side mirrors typically use:
questions.explanation: CONVEX MIRRORS (curved outward) used in vehicle side/rear-view mirrors. WHY: (1) Convex mirrors give a WIDER FIELD OF VIEW than plane mirrors of same size — see more area, important for spotting other vehicles. (2) IMAGE always virtual, erect, smaller (diminished). KEY: USA + Europe convex side mirrors are LEGALLY MANDATED on passenger cars to have a small flat 'spot mirror' nearby; some Indian cars also have this. CAUTION SIGN: 'OBJECTS IN MIRROR ARE CLOSER THAN THEY APPEAR' — because convex mirror DIMINISHES image, brain underestimates distance. CONVEX MIRROR uses (memorize): (1) VEHICLE side mirrors. (2) Mirrors at BLIND CORNERS (intersections, hospital corridors, supermarkets — security against theft). (3) MAGNIFYING glass reverse — convex mirror gives smaller image; concave gives larger. CONTRAST OF MIRROR USES: CONVEX (always virtual, erect, smaller) → wide-view applications. CONCAVE (varies by distance) → magnify (shaving), focus (headlights, telescopes). PLANE → simple reflection (regular mirrors). KEY: convex mirror has POSITIVE focal length (per many conventions; it's a DIVERGING mirror — extends rays outward). PRACTICE — UPSC / NEET style: identify mirror used in given application. (a) Telescope objective → CONCAVE. (b) Vehicle side mirror → CONVEX. (c) Bathroom mirror → PLANE. PYQ FREQUENCY: mirror-applications in NEET, NCERT, SSC 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: The relationship between FOCAL LENGTH (f) and RADIUS OF CURVATURE (R) of a SPHERICAL MIRROR is:

options.option_text: f = R/2 (focal length is half radius)

questions.explanation: f = R/2 — focal length is HALF the radius of curvature. This is the PARAXIAL approximation valid for SMALL ANGLE incidence near principal axis. PROOF: A ray parallel to the axis hitting the mirror at small angle from axis reflects through F. Geometry: triangle with apex at C (center), one side along axis (length R), other side from F (length R−f). For small angle: F is at midpoint between P and C → f = R/2. KEY: HOLDS for both CONCAVE (f, R both negative in Cartesian) and CONVEX (f, R both positive). EXAMPLES: (1) Mirror with R = 20 cm → f = 10 cm. (2) Mirror with R = 40 cm → f = 20 cm. (3) PLANE MIRROR — R = ∞ → f = ∞ (parallel rays remain parallel, never converge). KEY for SPHERICAL ABERRATION: at LARGER angles from axis, paraxial approximation BREAKS DOWN; rays don't all converge to single point → image becomes blurred. PARABOLOIDAL mirrors (mathematical paraboloid shape) avoid this — ALL parallel rays focus to single point. USE: telescopes, headlights, satellite dishes use parabolic reflectors. WHY SPHERICAL (not paraboloidal) used in many cases? Easier and cheaper to make spheres than paraboloids. INDUSTRIAL MIRROR MAKING: silvering process — coat glass back-surface with silver/aluminum. PYQ FREQUENCY: f = R/2 in NEET, NCERT, JEE-Main 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: A PERISCOPE used in submarines works on the principle of:

options.option_text: Total internal reflection in prisms or two-mirror system
Refraction through convex lens only (option here)
Diffraction of light through gaps (option here)
Polarization of light by sunlight (option here)

questions.explanation: PERISCOPE — instrument that allows OBSERVATION OVER OBSTACLES. SIMPLE PERISCOPE: two PLANE MIRRORS at 45° in a tube, top mirror reflects external scene DOWN; bottom mirror reflects DOWN-incoming light HORIZONTALLY into observer's eye. Each mirror angle = 45°; total ray-deviation = 180° (back to viewer). MILITARY PERISCOPES (submarines): use PRISMS (right-angled, isoceles) instead of mirrors — utilize TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION inside the prism (each face acts as a perfect reflector, no metallic coating needed). WHY PRISMS BETTER: (a) No silver/aluminum coating to wear off / get damaged. (b) Higher reflectivity (~100% vs ~95% for mirrors). (c) More durable. SUBMARINE PERISCOPES: 10-15 m long; can periscope-up while submerged at periscope depth (~15 m); used for visual observation of surface. MODERN SUBMARINES: replacing periscopes with NON-PENETRATING ELECTRO-OPTICAL MASTS — cameras + sensors + radio + GPS in a mast that doesn't penetrate the pressure hull (no need for vertical sight tube through submarine). EXAMPLES: USA Virginia-class subs, India's INS ARIHANT. PERISCOPE in TANKS/ARMORED VEHICLES — for safe observation. CIVILIAN USES: observing crowds, tall barriers. PYQ FREQUENCY: periscope in NEET, NCERT, SSC GA 1× per cycle.
